title: The Cyrillic Stalemate: Why Uzbekistan’s Alphabet Reform is Still Stuck 30 Years Later
author: Dolunay Yusuf Baltürk
text:
A roadside checkpoint marked “Nazorat Posti 5” (“Checkpoint 5”), photographed in Uzbekistan. The sign provides a simple example of the Latin script’s presence in everyday public life, where it is now widely used for routine administrative, commercial and public signage.
Credit: Dolunay Yusuf Baltürk
Uzbekistan’s transition from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet is not merely a technical change; rather, it has a far-reaching dimension tied to the nation-building process. Since declaring its independence in 1991, Tashkent has revised its alphabet policies numerous times, yet the simultaneous use of both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets has continued for over 30 years.Visitors to Uzbekistan will still see both alphabets — alongside the Russian language, which uses a Cyrillic alphabet – in many parts of daily life. [...]
